speechtext: Apologize.

We have no reason to apologize with the stuff that has been coming from that side of the House. You should take a lesson on your own.
The Government has made commitments in the past that there would be assurances that safe countries would be safe for claimants who would be sent to those countries. The Minister talked about guarantees, then changed his tune and talked about arrangements. Now we have an amendment that would suggest there would be an agreement with those countries which would purportedly suggest that they are safe.
We moved motions suggesting the removal of the prescreening stage rooted in a safe country concept. Those motions were defeated and we now ask the Government to support its own Member, the Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), who is currently the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration.
If it will not abandon the safe country concept or allow the refugee division to draft a safe country list, and if it will not agree that a list to be drafted by the Cabinet would only serve in an advisory capacity, the very least we are asking of the Government through this motion is that any member country on the safe country list have a written invalidating agreement with Canada before that safe country list is drawn in order to ensure the Cabinet and all Canadians of that country's safety.
I think that would be a valuable asset and a welcomed modification to the Bill. When an individual is sent to a so-called safe country, at least we can be assured that it is safe on the grounds of that written agreement between the two countries. We do not want to leave the word "safe" too loosely defined or leave open the question of return as opposed to admission because, as we have said so often, in many cases it is a question of life versus death. It is a question of a human being trying to find a country where he or she may find some basic human rights.
I suggest that if any of us were put in the same precarious situation we would want the same for our families.
It is one thing to try to make a system better, but when we talk about a safe country, there is the knowledge that we are


Immigration Act, 1976
sending someone away from our shores. Knowing we are passing the responsibility to someone else, the very least we can do is offer some morality and leadership so that if we are sending someone away from our shores we know we are sending them to a country which is going to extend a hand of compassion, assistance and welcome, that there is that partnership and the Geneva Convention will still be intact. If we legislate a safe country concept without grounding it in agreements and ensuring safety, then we will be driving a wedge into the Geneva Convention, which will mean its worth is on paper, but when it comes to practice there is no Convention to speak of.
Let us move forward as a country and show our leadership internationally Let us reclaim the leadership Canada has demonstrated over the years. Let us offer other countries an incentive and, perhaps, an inspiration to follow its best instincts domestically, regardless of the challenges and pressures from within.
This motion would try to mobilize these countries, to open a dialogue. If we are going to go "safe country", let us ensure the reciprocating country has the same standards, that a refugee from El Salvador will be treated with the same respect they receive in Canada, Belgium or Great Britain. There is an opportunity for Canada-apart from calling for an international summit-through this small motion, to say to the world; let us do it in partnership, let us do it in tandem. Therefore, I urge Members of the House, particularly government Members, to agree with this very last motion, and perhaps then the report stage will begin on an upbeat.
Perhaps I should take this moment as well, Mr. Speaker, to correct my earlier reference to the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). If the reasons were because of the Jewish holiday, then I would be the last to fault him for that. If I have caused any embarrassment to himself or to his community, I am very sorry about that.

I rise to support motion No. 75 in the name of the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais). I wish to take this occasion, as others have, to congratulate the Hon. Member for his strong conviction and courage in taking the stand he has as a dissident with his caucus on this point. I also wish to congratulate the Progressive Conservative caucus for having accommodated the Hon. Member. I know this was done in consultation and that it was not an easy consultation. I know there has been much heart searching on the part of the Hon. Member and his caucus colleagues in the difficult situation created for all of them by the conscientious disagreement of the Hon. Member for La Prairie with his hon. colleagues. Therefore, I respect the fact that it has been possible to carry on in spite of the sharp disagreement between the Hon. Member and his colleagues, and that is to the credit of the Progressive Conservative caucus.
On this motion I wish to take the same position taken by the two previous speakers, but to emphasize a little further the great importance of having this clause protected in order to carry out what may well be the intention of the Government. This intention is not sufficiently protected in the wording, and so far as I can find out in this complicated Bill-which has been revised a good deal by the Government-is not adequately protected elsewhere.
Some effort was made in amendments earlier in committee to get this amended by way of a fuller statement of the Convention obligations. That was refused. Some effort was made to have the adjudicator and the refugee division member made responsible for deciding in the inquiry the specific country to which the person would be sent. That was turned down. Efforts were made to have the matter adequately reviewed after a decision in order to catch possible errors, including an error of sending a person to a country that was not genuinely safe, particularly if the person thought it was not genuinely safe. That was turned down.
We now have a proposal that seems entirely in accord with what the Minister and his colleagues have said. The Minister said passionately in the debate in June that a person would not be sent to any country without a clear understanding. He used words like "agreement, guarantee, arrangement". He said there would be clear understanding that he or she would be given the same protection they would have in Canada. But that is not in the Bill. It is not in this clause and I believe it is not anywhere else in the Bill.
We are simply asking now that the clause be revised, that is, the clause describing the duty of the Minister to write the regulations, so that he will prescribe:
-for the purposes of paragraph 48.1 (1 )(b), any country with which Canada has a written arrangement with respect to persons who are or who claim to be Convention refugees as a safe third country for all persons or for persons of a specified class of persons, having regard to the record of that country with respect to human rights and to expulsion of persons who are or who claim to be Convention refugees.
I believe the wording is the same as the Government's wording excepting the words concerning the written arrangement. I believe that will not cause a breakdown of the system. It will not cause endless legal disputes. It will not be a loophole for bogus refugees. It is within the control of the Government to make that clear, to make it clear in such a way that the refugee claimant who is being sent away to that country, and all who are concerned with him, and all who are concerned with the integrity of the system, will know how the system is operating and, if necessary, will be able to offer an opinion and disagreement. If country x is listed as a safe country because of a written agreement, the written agreement can be looked at in public and questioned, perhaps altered or perhaps defended and maintained. That would be a democratic procedure.
I hope the Government will give serious consideration to this amendment. I know that officials and some members of the Government are concerned about trying to arrange with some of the countries in western Europe, perhaps the United States,


and no doubt some other countries, a system in which one occasion for determining a person's refugee status would be enough for all who would belong to a certain agreement.
If a person was found to be a refugee in this country, that would stand for the others. If he was found not to be a refugee, that would stand for the others. I know that is being attempted and I think it is well worth attempting. I also know agreement has not yet been arrived at. Written agreements of this sort might be a step in that direction. At least they would provide some basis of agreement between Canada and one other country in bilateral agreements. They might eventually be put together into a multilateral agreement. I, therefore, urge the Government to consider this amendment in a very friendly way.
Finally, I want to refer to a voice of the Canadian people- not "the" voice because there is no single voice-but a very strong voice of the Canadian people which has supported many of the amendments in spirit and sometimes explicitly throughout this debate. I am referring to the letter of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops dated September 16. I wish to quote a resolution that was passed at their meeting. It concerns the refugee status determination process in Canada, and it states:
Whereas the Government of Canada is currently finalizing Bill C-55, an Act dealing with the refugee status determination process in Canada;
Whereas Bill C-84 has just passed third reading (September 14, 1987), in spite of the reservations and opposition of a multitude of humanitarian, refugee aid, and church groups.
The Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs recommends to the Plenary Assembly:
That during the course of the daily press conference, the President of the CCCB recall the position taken by Canadian Church leaders in their telex message of June 1, 1987, to Prime Minister Mulroney which called for the withdrawal of Bill C-55 and the replacing of it with legislation that will actualize a refugee status determination process which is just, workable, expeditious and respectful of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in conformity with Canada's international responsibilities as a signator of the Geneva Convention.
This is the proposal of the Most Reverend Gilles Ouellet, Chairman, Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs.
We have strong support for taking the more inclusive and humanitarian approach to the definition of our refugee legislation. I urge Hon. Members opposite to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, first I welcome the presence of the Minister and applaud the fact that he found it possible to be here with us today.
We speak in support of the motion of the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), because an important principle is at stake. With his amendment, the Hon. Member is defending the internationally accepted principle of prohibiting the expulsion or the return of an applicant for refugee status by any country.
Immigration Act, 1976
In 1969 we agreed to an international convention.
For the record, I wish to quote Article 33 which deals exactly with this matter. It is entitled Prohibition of Expulsion or Return ("Refoulement") and it states:
1.	No Contracting State shall expel or return ("refouler") a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.
Article 33 is well balanced. In paragraph 2 it states:
2.	The benefit of the present provision may not, however, be claimed by a refugee whom there are reasonable grounds for regarding as a danger to the security of the country in which he is, or who, having been convicted by a final judgment of a particularly serious crime, constitutes a danger to the community of that country.
Article 33 is very reasonable, and it was put forward during an international convention that we subscribed to.
During the hearings, the Canadian Bar Association expressed an opinion on the present Bill, and its dissatisfaction if the Bill were to go ahead without the protection of this principle, which would be taken care of by the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for La Prairie. The Canadian Bar Association stated that if this Bill is allowed to exclude the safe country notion, it would violate Article 33 of the UN Convention on Refugees because it rejects the claimant without considering whether the person is a refugee. This is an important central principle. The nub of the issue is that it requires the removal of that person without assurances that the country of destination will protect him from being returned to his original country where the danger may be.
We are dealing with a very important principle. We hope that the Minister and the Government will agree with a member of their own caucus, the Chairman of the standing committee, who has put forward this very important amendment which goes to the heart of any legislation that deals with refugees.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, September 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak this afternoon on Bill C-74 which has been put forward as the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. There is serious concern in the country about the inadequacy of this legislation. It is unfortunate that the Government did not, in drafting this legislation, seriously attempt to provide environmental protection.
The title of this Bill is definitely a misnomer. If the Government insists on proceeding with this legislation in its present


form, the Opposition will fight to remove the name "Canadian Environmental Protection Act".
This Bill pays lip-service to the protection of the environment while overlooking the serious attacks which have been made on our environment. This is not leadership legislation. It is a desperate attempt to appease people, and it will certainly not work. Canadians are seriously concerned about the erosion of the environment. They are concerned that they do not have a safe and healthy place in which to raise their children. They are concerned that there is no effective forum in which to raise environmental concerns where they can get a fair hearing and an effective response. Such a forum does not exist now and will not exist should this legislation be passed.
When this Bill is finally sent to committee the members of the committee will have a monstrous task in attempting to provide legislation which will ensure that Canadians will have an opportunity to be directly involved in the protection of the environment.
There is no issue as important to Canadians as environmental protection. What does any other issue matter if diseases which develop and physical harm which is inflicted upon people through contamination of the environment are allowed to continue? Of what importance is any other issue? Over a period of time many Canadians have come to realize that this issue is far more important than many others which face us today.
We hope that the Government will pay heed to the concerns expressed by Members of Parliament on behalf of their constituents. We hope that the Government will listen carefully to the analyses of groups across Canada which have been fighting on environmental issues for years. We hope that this Bill will be redrafted to take cognizance of the points raised.
This is not legislation to protect the environment. Through this legislation the Government is attempting only to protect its backside on this critical issue. It is attempting to protect its backside for its failure to deal with environmental issues vitally important to Canadians. This is not an environmental protection Act. It must be reworked in committee to make it into a tool which Canadians can use to protect themselves, a tool which will guarantee that children will grow up safe and healthy protected from environmental contamination and the destruction of our environment.
This legislation is simply an amalgamation of existing laws in an attempt to sell them as something new and wonderful. Those who are concerned about the degradation of the environment which has gone on over the years will not be fooled by this legislation. They will recognize that it is not a tool to effect that protection.
It has been suggested that this legislation should contain an environmental bill of rights, a clear statement of what Canadians are entitled to in terms of environmental protection and standards. It should be a statement of our goals and
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
objectives. There is no clear statement in the legislation of what it is trying to achieve. It is critical to have such a clear statement to guide the decisions of administrators who set standards and impose emergency orders to protect the environment. Tjiere is no doubt that this Bill must state its objectives clearly. On that basis Canadians can make a judgment about the Government's political will to provide a safe, clean environment. This Bill rrjust state that Canadians have the right to a safe, clean environment.
There is very little provision in this legislation of opportunities for the public to participate in the enforcement of environmental laws. There are many people in this country who are seriously concerned about the degradation of the environment.
In the area which I represent people have formed groups protesting the use of herbicides and pesticides. They have come out to meetings to state that they do not want this stuff used near their homes, that they do not want it sprayed aerially or dropped in their water systems. They are frustrated in their attempts to express these concerns or to have a serious hearing on them. People have obstructed applicators in the process of using these chemicals in the environment, but they have no effective forum in which to prosecute abuses and infractions actively.
The public must have an opportunity to participate in the enforcement of environmental legislation. They must be able to become actively involved in prosecuting those who commit environmental infractions, whether it be misuse of herbicides and pesticides, misuse of dangerous chemicals, or oil and chemical spills. People do not have effective mechanisms by which they can initiate action. The public cannot go to the court in order to resolve successfully any challenges to imposed standards.
We must address the need to provide a forum for effective public participation in setting environmental standards for the communities in which they live. They should have the right to determine the quality of the environment in their areas and the Government should encourage involvement in that process by providing an effective forum.
1 believe that the application of chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides should only be done with the co-operation of local people who would determine the standards of use. This legislation should provide for such a mechanism.
For instance, there is the use of pesticides and herbicides in school playgrounds. 1 would be absolutely irate if my children were in areas with that material and I had no opportunity to oppose its use. I am sure all Hon. Members would agree with other Canadians on that issue.
This situation also exists with respect to the use of pesticides by those who advocate aerial spraying of forests. The area of Okeover Inlet is an example of this situation. The federal Government licenses the product, the provincial Government


Canadian Environmental Protection Act
claims no responsibility because it has been licensed by the federal Government, and there is no consideration for the individuals who live there.
The decision was made to use a helicopter to spray an area that was sensitive in terms of the watershed and the marine environment. It is one of the major shellfish-raising areas in British Columbia which had not been contaminated. Residents eventually threatened that they would shoot down any helicopter carrying pesticides that was flying over the area. Of course, this elicited the appropriate response from the RCMP, who defused the situation, but it illustrates the frustration experienced by people when the Government refuses to listen to their concerns about their children and the quality of the environment in which they live. The people of that community banded together and managed to convince the Government that they would remove the unwanted material themselves. They obtained a federal government grant and removed the alder by hand.
The basic problem in this situation was that they had no sense of effective participation in the decision on the use of those chemicals in that area.
We have seen similar cases up and down the coast of British Columbia, whether it is Fanny Bay, Merville, or the Sechelt Peninsula. Hundreds of people have attended public meetings to voice their outrage because a major corporation like B.C. Hydro, MacMillan Bloedel or Crown Forest Products have been able to use these materials with provincial government approval that is based on the federal government sanction. The people affected by these chemicals have no say in the standards for licensing those chemicals. They have no effective say in where those chemicals will be applied.
The Bill should provide Canadians with a fair opportunity to be involved in the setting of standards for these chemicals and where and how they will be applied. It would be a great service to Canada and the quality of our environment if that were one of the strong features of this legislation.
1 believe that dangerous chemicals as defined in this legislation will not include pesticides and herbicides, which has been a source of great aggravation to Canadians over the years.
The Department of Agriculture has had the responsibility for licensing these products in Canada. Apparently, it has used tests in the United States to determine the acceptability of these chemicals in Canada. While the provincial Government determines how the chemicals are used, federal government licensing entitles its use.
Many Canadians have suggested that some of these licensed chemicals are in fact toxic and affect human beings. Only recently, the Canadian Government admitted that chemicals such as 2,4-D are harmful to human health. Canadians have appealed to the Government to remove many other herbicide and pesticide products from agriculture. Such chemicals should be included in the Environmental Protection Act to
illustrate that the Government is concerned about their use and that it will encourage public participation in determining how and when these chemicals will be used if they are acceptable.
The Department of Agriculture should no longer be entitled to set the standards, because there is a major conflict of interest. Most Canadians would support this legislation if it were expanded to include herbicides and pesticides that are used widely in Canada, and I hope Members on the committee will broaden the legislation to include that class of chemicals.
Another area of major concern is the setting of national standards. I believe this Bill pays only lip-service to a major problem and does not provide any new initiatives in environmental protection.
Certain clauses of the Bill require the Government to consult with the provinces before setting national standards. The Social Credit Government of British Columbia has done much to erode environmental protection in Canada. While there is nothing wrong with consultation between federal and provincial Governments with respect to environmental standards, there should be a minimum national standard for the protection of the health of Canadians below which no provincial Government will be allowed to go. Where provinces are prepared to put higher standards in place, more effective procedures, that consultation should be an area of fair operation. There should even be federal assistance to ensure that those kinds of higher standards are encouraged and supported.
It would be our hope that this consultation section would be tightened so it was effective consultation and there would not be the ability to destroy federal standards or erode those standards and delay application. It is an absolute must that there be national standards, that the federal Government have the political will to enforce those standards, and that provinces which seek to impose higher standards in special areas receive encouragement and support from the federal Government. This issue is of enormous importance.
There is mention in Clause 38 that provincial consultation on matters of emergency orders are being put in place. It would appear that the federal Government has almost lost its political nerve at this point. With respect to an emergency order which involves, I would contemplate, an oil spill or spill of toxic chemicals in the marine environment-we have been treated to many serious oil spills in the Province of British Columbia-to suggest that the federal Government, before it acts on a toxic chemical spill in the provincial environment, should not have to consult with the Province of British Columbia.
I see that my time is drawing nigh. Hopefully, the important points that have been raised on the shortcomings of this legislation will be the subject of committee study, particularly


in the herbicides and pesticides area. Action must be taken on those issue before this Bill has been passed into law.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? There being no questions, debate. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson).
I have a question, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry, I recognized the Hon. Member for Western Arctic.

Mr. Speaker, while in general I am in favour of the provisions of Bill C-74, and I think that most of the Members of the House of Commons are,
1 want to bring to the attention of the Houses two specific areas outlined in this Bill that might need further study.
The first is really a constitutional matter. I am referring to the powers and authorities of the Government of Canada to regulate environmental matters in the Northwest Territories and Yukon, as opposed to what, in my opinion, ought to be the case. The people who live there, through their elected representatives on the Legislatures of the two Territories ought to be the ones, the same as the people in a province ought to make the overriding rules and regulations respecting environmental protection. Part IV of the Bill is the part that deals with federal Departments, agencies, Crown corporations, works, undertakings and lands. When it talks about federal lands, what it really means is all the land in the Northwest Territories and all the land in Yukon. We are at the bottom of the list after federal Departments and agencies and Crown corporations.
The operative clause in this part of the Bill is Clause 53. What it does is to empower the Governor in Council to make regulations with respect to virtually anything to do with the environment on those lands. We are going to run into some problems there, that 1 know. One of the problems will, of course, be battles between the Department of the Environment and the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs, which already likes to think it is the agency or Department that regulates with respect to these matters, and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which also has some responsibility in that area. I know there will be an interdepartmental battle between those Departments of Government.
There is in the Northwest Territories an Act of the Territorial Legislature called the NWT Environmental Protection Act, I believe. It has never really had much attention because of all these federal regulations that are in effect and that have been administered by various government Departments. I think it would be preferable if the NWT Environmental Protection Act were the one under which prosecution were made, the one which is primarily used to regulate and enforce environmental matters in the Territories. That would be in keeping with the policy of the Parliament of Canada, both the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada, which
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
wants to see provincial types of responsibilities devolve to the Territories.
It seems that this Bill is in some way drawing back from that policy. We have made some rapid strides of late with respect to electrical power, medical services and forestry, but we have recently been hit with the Meech Lake Agreement which has taken away something from us. It would appear to me that Bill C-74 would also tend to do the same thing.
I want to register my objections to this and my suggestion that things might proceed in a direction more in keeping with that given by the Parliament of Canada on previous occasions.
The second point I wish to raise arises from a meeting I had a few days ago with Mr. Walter Kudelik, the President of the Northwest Territories Association of Municipalities. I have a letter from his Executive Director, Mr. Jim Pitt of that association that I would like to read into the record. It is addressed to myself and states as follows:
Enclosed with this letter is correspondence pertaining to Bill C-74 (Environmental Protection Act) and its impact on municipal liability insurance. The NWTAM's insurance consultant, Mr. Hugh Falconar has expressed grave concerns about the implications Bill C-74 will have for our members; we want you to be aware of these concerns.
It goes on to say that they have contacted the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to request some additional information and assistance. I also have a letter from Mr. Hugh Falconar, insurance consultant to the NWT Association of Municipalities, dated July 28. Mr. Falconar gives his opinion that:
The Bill, a minefield for municipalities, appears to be a goldfield for federal prosecutors. The implications of Clause 116(1) are awesome.
It goes on to say further in the letter:
At the moment, the absolute pollution exclusions in the general liability and umbrella liability insurance policies eliminate all pollution protection for municipalities.
If Bill C-74 were enacted without the municipalities being able to have the benefit of insurance protection or some form of contingency funding, municipalities would be put into an almost impossible situation.
I do not know if the situation is quite as bad as Mr. Falconar believes because, of course, we have to read Clause 116 in conjunction with Clause 117, which gives some defence. But I think there is something to be concerned about in his remarks.
I also understand that the Canadian Water and Waste Water Association has been involved in the early stages of the drafting of the Bill, and I am pleased to see that this has taken place. I hope that when this goes to committee the Canadian Water and Waste Water Association will be invited to make further presentations and suggestions as to the manner in which the Bill may be improved.
In the Northwest Territories, there is case law under the Canada Labour Code that has held that municipalities are federal works or undertakings. It is pretty hard to believe that this is true, but it has happened. That is why municipalities in


Canadian Environmental Protection Act
the Northwest Territories, and presumably also in the Yukon, are likely to be affected more by this Bill than municipalities elsewhere in Canada. It is a great concern.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to urge Members of the House to adopt this Bill in principle and send it on to the Agriculture Committee for full-scale study and hearings.
The Bill deals with very important concerns which we have as Members from across the country, whether we represent urban or rural constituencies or, as I do, constituencies with a combination of the two. The debt situation of farmers is one sign of the crisis which they have been facing. It is a steadily worsening debt situation. What is particularly striking is that the debt situation is especially falling on larger farms which are the backbone of production in most parts of the country and, perhaps most tragic, on young farmers.
According to the official statistics, only 26 per cent of younger operators of farms under the age of 35 years report no interest expenses, whereas 61 per cent of older operators, 55 years of age and over, report no interest expenses.
We are talking about something in the order of $2 billion per year which is going from farm families in the form of interest, resulting in a reduction in the number of farmers on farms. For instance, in Ontario the number of younger farmers under the age of 35 years has declined by 22 per cent. Between 1981 and 1986 the capital value of farms has gone down by 16 per cent. In my Province of Ontario the decline has been an even steeper 24 per cent.
What do we do in the face of those facts? It is important to recognize the principle of parity pricing which is embodied in the Bill. That principle says that the prices which farmers get for their products, in so far as we can have some influence on them in domestic markets in Canada, should go up in proportion to the costs of production that farmers must face.
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
I should like to refer to the catastrophic situation facing Ontario farmers which Calls for this kind of move to parity pricing. I know that the Bill itself does not deal with corn or soya beans. However, in his opening speech the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) indicated that he had met with producers of both commodities and could certainly see ways within the committee that these commodities could be brought into the Bill. For instance, let us take corn production and the price as of just yesterday in Chatham. Farmers in southwestern Ontario are receiving $2.27 per bushel. There are small variations to $2.37 or $2.47 in some parts of southwestern Ontario, but the $2.27 per bushel figure compares with a cost of production estimated by the provincial Government of $3.48 per bushel, including materials, pre-harvest expenses, harvest expenses, and land rent or the cost of land.
Dealing with the soya bean crop, in 1980 we started with a market price of $8.53. We have seen that figure decline to a market price per bushel of $6.20 in 1987. That compares with a cost production of $7.80.
Therefore we have a situation where farmers continue hoping for the future, but because of the difference between the prices they are receiving and costs of production, they are going more and more into debt and facing further and further difficulties for themselves and their families.
We must have a solution to this serious crisis, and I think the solution can come with the creation of marketing boards for commodities such as soya beans and corn on the domestic market. It can come with the recognition in those marketing boards that there must be a continued reflection in the prices offered by the boards of the costs of production and how they are increasing in my part of Ontario and in other parts of Ontario.
I urge the House to recognize what many of us recognized in the all-night debate which took place last spring. It indicated that there was a crisis in agriculture, but we have still not responded to that crisis sufficiently despite the drama of that all-night debate.
Let us take action. Let us move ahead. Let us do something concrete. Let us adopt Bill C-221. Let us take the step forward which this Bill represents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this Bill in that my riding contains some of the finest black loam farmland in Canada.
The intent of the Bill is well recognized. There is consensus across Canada that farmers deserve and should receive a fair and equitable return on their investment and labour. However, there is no one Bill that can assure adequate returns to all farmers of Canada at all times. There is no single program that will achieve that goal, least of all Bill C-221 respecting parity prices for farm products. This concept, which was used in the United States over 45 years ago, was eventually discontinued due to major shortcomings. It could be an


Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
opportune time to review the U.S. system of parity prices and its consequences.
The parity formula in the U.S. was established in 1940 by the Agricultural Adjustment Act. The purpose of the Act was to establish farm prices at a level that would maintain the purchasing power of farmers, with respect to articles they buy, equivalent to that of the base period. However, in order for purchasing power to be maintained over time, relative prices and incomes in the base period must be appropriate. In the United States it became apparent that there were substantial income differences among farmers, no matter what base period was used.
The intent of the parity pricing Act in the United States was similar to that of Bill C-221 in respect of adjusting prices of farm commodities to reflect changes in the prices of the articles which farmers buy. However, Mr. Speaker, being a scholar of the subject you will know that in order to stabilize supplies and prices, parity prices were incorporated into the loan rate formula. Farmers sold what they could, and the rest was purchased and stored by the Government. As technology advanced, production increased faster than demand. This increased the need for price support and over-production problems became unmanageable. Eventually, the Investment Parity Price Support Program became so expensive that it was disbanded.
It is interesting to note that although costs associated with the parity formula grew significantly, farmers were often not at the receiving end. Much of the money went to transportation, storage agencies and construction companies. The U.S. experience illustrated that parity prices were not effective in providing price support to farmers. It cost billions of dollars, only a portion of which went to farmers.
Bill C-221 is primarily aimed at helping Canadian grain and oil-seed producers who are experiencing a very difficult time. They are in a cost-price squeeze where market prices are falling and input costs are rising. As an example, wheat prices have fallen about 30 per cent in the last year due largely to an international trade war, while input prices have remained the same or even increased. Grain farmers on the Prairies are expected to experience a net decline in farm income this year, although this decline is being offset to a large degree through payments under government programs.
The solution to the farm income problem would not be solved by Bill C-221. The U.S. experience indicates that eventually it would be detrimental to the agriculture industry. The idea of parity pricing does not take into account new technology, efficiency of production, market signals and the need for international product marketability. It ignores the dynamic and often unpredictable nature of the agriculture industry due to such diverse forces and conflicting interests, regionally, nationally, and internationally. Over the past years, the farm sector in Canada has been effectively served by
programs that increased the efficiency and competitiveness of farmers in the market-place, both nationally and internationally. A legislated solution will not be responsive to constantly changing circumstances and will therefore result in high costs with declining effectiveness.
One can argue that national supply management agencies in place for dairy and poultry products serve that industry well and that the same arrangement could apply to grains and oilseeds. But these agencies have been established at the direct request of producers themselves who continue to recognize the fluctuating nature of the markets. They have built-in flexibility to protect both producers and consumers. Bill C-221 would not allow the same conditions for the grain and oil-seed producers. To be efficient and competitive, the market forces of supply and demand must prevail. That has always been a fundamental philosophy behind agricultural policy in Canada, a philosophy shared by all provinces as signatories to the recently developed national agriculture strategy.
The Government has been working with provincial administrations and the farm industry to build a network of programs to strengthen the productivity, efficiency and competitiveness of agriculture industry while providing farm income protection. Special initiatives have been introduced to help producers who are experiencing difficulties. In the long run, this approach will provide the best protection against the cost-price squeeze experienced by the Canadian agriculture sector.
Some of the support programs provided for Canadian grain and oil-seed farmers are the Special Canadian Grains Program, providing $1 billion this year to assist the grain and oilseed farmers who have been facing lower prices resulting from the agricultural trade war between the United States and the European Economic Community. Payments are being made under the Agricultural Stabilization Act to farmers affected by lower prices, including close to $55.8 million for corn, soybean and barley producers for their 1985-86 crop. Special assistance was provided to prairie grain and livestock producers who suffered from the effects of several consecutive years of drought. The Western Grain Stabilization Act has been amended to allow interim payments to farmers in the spring when they need the cash most. An interim payment of $705 million has been made in 1986-87 for the last crop year. A tripartite stabilization program for the red meat sector has been established, with six provinces participating and others being expected to join. Participating provinces now represent between two-thirds and three-quarters of all beef cattle, sheep and hog production in the nation. This program is helping to stabilize returns for red meat producers, without shielding them from market signals. The Farm Fuel Tax Rebate Program exempts farmers from federal sales and excise taxes on farm fuels. An $80 million, five-year interest rate relief program has been designed and implemented to lower the interest costs for more than 5,000 Farm Credit Corporation borrowers. The two new FCC lending programs recently introduced are allowing farmers much greater financial flexibility.


These initiatives represent an innovative approach to protecting farmers from the current cost-price squeeze. They have been developed and implemented to respond to specific conditions in the market, and they reflect the flexibility and responsiveness required to deal with specific problems. This process is most effective in serving the interests of the agriculture sector as problems arise. The parity price system would not serve the industry as well and could result in continuing high costs to the taxpayer. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I regret that I am not able to support the spirit and the essence of Bill C-221.

What is at issue here, and clearly at issue, is fairness. Anyone who looks at the situation faced by the farmers in Canada could by no means conclude that the farmer is treated with fairness. This is not deliberate, but if you compared the situation of the farmer as he and she experiences it now and contemplated just for a moment the prospects for the future, then one would have to reach the conclusion that we must search our collective minds to find the means by which the farmer will be able to obtain an adequate income.
No one suggests that this piece of legislation proposed here now is the entire answer to the problems that farmers face. It does go a little way, and it is a little way, that collectively all of us must walk.
I have said on a previous occasion when addressing the concerns of the agricultural community that I admit to being an urban representative. It occurs to me that there is a very significant industry in my riding called Hiram Walker. It consumes a great deal of barley and wheat. We will not say anything further about the manner in which the product is consumed and by whom and in what quantity here and elsewhere, but what we should address is that not a single worker in Hiram Walker faces as serious a deficit in income as does the farmer who provides the basis for that worker's livelihood. Nobody really expects a worker or a business person to continue carrying out his or her business or work under circumstances where he or she cannot make a profit. I repeat, this is about fairness.
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
I think we can all agree that it is not fair that the price of wheat for export will decrease by 20 per cent. It is not fair that it will cost a farmer $69,000 to produce wheat on 1,000 acres but he can only expect to make $40,000 from it. It is not fair that farmers are losing their farms, that the family farm is disappearing because of inadequate income and huge debt and that in many instances young farmers have no hope of owning a farm. It is not fair that in the area in which I live, the producers of soybeans and corn, the most common commodities produced in that area, find that it costs them more to produce their commodities than they can sell them for. They earn $2 per bushel for corn while it costs $3 per bushel to produce it, and they earn $6 per bushel for soybeans while it costs $7 per bushel to produce it. That is not fair, and what we are talking about here is fairness.
What is so strange, unusual and unreasonable about the proposition advanced in this Bill that wheat, oats and barley sold to the Canadian consumer should be priced so that the cost of production is covered? The production costs that should be covered include good wages for city workers and good profits for those producing implements and vehicles used on farms. That is all this Bill seeks to provide through what is called parity pricing. The farmer who sells his wheat, oats and barley should receive a return adequate to cover the cost of production and should earn a profit sufficient to allow the farmer to live, to eat and to clothe himself and his family. Why should the farmer provide to all the rest of us what we so desperately and continuously need at his own expense?
Is the proposition contained in the Bill not a self-evident one? Is this not something that all of us would naturally assume is a simple matter of justice and fairness? As the Hon. Member from the other side who spoke indicated, there are some small elements of the legislation that need to be adjusted to make it good legislation. I for one, coming from Essex County, would like to see it extended so that it would apply to soybean and corn producers. Just as wheat, barley and oats concern those in the West and in parts of Ontario, we in southwestern Ontario have a problem as well.
As well, I think note should be taken that there is a proposal here for marketing boards for beef and pork. Although that is not being demanded, it may be that we would want to prepare the way so that those producers too could share in the benefits of the simple principle advanced by this legislation, which is that one should not have to produce food for city people at one's own expense.
I urge the House to approve the submission of this Bill to the Agriculture Committee so that it can be refined and made practical and useful and so that it can benefit the farmer. I am as confident as I am confident that I am standing here today that, given an understanding of the situation faced by farmers, those in the cities would not expect the farmer to earn less than the automobile worker, the brewer or the politician in proportion to their contribution to this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to be able to speak to Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for farm products.
Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, the electors of the riding of Windsor-Walkerville had an opportunity to listen to their Member or will find time to read his comments in Hansard. They will see for themselves that the Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) was not very serious when he spoke to this legislative measure.
Mr. Speaker, setting the prices of farm products at the so-called parity level is one way to establish a link between these prices and the cost index of the agricultural community's input.
The concept of parity prices was used in a U.S. farm legislation some forty years ago. Its purpose was to establish farm prices at a level that would maintain the purchasing power of farmers, with respect to articles they buy, equivalent to that of the base period.
To determine the parity price of a farm commodity during a period prior to this base period, they would multiply its price during the base period by the input cost index reached during the period when the computation was made.
However, this procedure did not take into account a basic factor, namely, that as technology advances, productivity increases steadily over the years.
Well, the input cost index reflects the trend of input prices and not the input mix during production. With the passing of time, technology advance makes it possible to combine inputs in a more efficient way and, in the end, smaller amounts of inputs are necessary to produce the same quantity of farm commodities. The unit cost goes down. Parity prices, therefore, may reach levels which are much higher than the costs to efficient farmers.
That is the reason why the parity price system was dropped in the United States.
Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for farm products, tries to overcome this problem by proposing to establish the prices on an annually established production cost formula.
By fixing prices on a yearly production cost basis, production cost pricing, although simple in principle, is not simple in its implementation. First, production costs have to be defined, which Bill C-221 does not do.
For instance, a distinction must be drawn between disbursement costs and non-disbursement costs. The difference is significant both conceptually and as to how costs are assessed.
The remuneration of the producer's work and investment entails no disbursement, but must be included in any pricing process.
One problem then is that, by determining farm prices on the basis of production costs, there is a danger that they be set at a level where demand will not completely absorb supply.
High prices stimulate production, Mr. Speaker, but on the other hand they discourage consumption. A pricing system based on a production cost formula cannot be put in place without a plan to limit supply to the level the available markets can absorb. Otherwise, the impact on external trade would be serious.
Mr. Speaker, providing a commodity with a high support price becomes costly when a country produces more of that commodity than it consumes. The surplus must be exported, and when world prices are still lower than domestic prices, this surplus is exported at a loss.
Such is the situation in the European Economic Community, and the common farm policy, which is the cause of that, is extremely costly to European taxpayers.
Canadian farm prices must be at a level that allows competition with foreign products. Otherwise, our products would not sell abroad because they would not compete on international markets. And then, if Canada used a double price system, selling abroad at prices that would be lower than domestic prices, it would be accused of dumping.
We cannot both develop the exportation of a product and introduce a parity prices system for that same product. Programs that are in place now, including the Western grain stabilization program and the tripartite stabilization programs that benefit beef, pork and lamb producers, better serve the needs of the export oriented production sectors then the parity prices system. They give a protection against downturns that periodically occur in the markets while ensuring that production be responsive to market trends.
So, Mr. Speaker, for these reasons and many others, it is absolutely unthinkable to implement a policy such as proposed by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) in his Bill C-221 and that is why we will have to vote against such a proposal since it is a socialist measure that would give no benefit to producers other than to burden them with enormous inconveniences, which is certainly not what we have been seeking since we came to power. Rather, we are working to help our producers become more and more efficient, more and more competitive so that they can carve out a significant place for themselves in the market so that ultimately we will succeed in stabilizing some sectors of productions by having profitable operations.

The purpose of this Bill is to provide parity prices to farmers based on a
cost-of-production formula for wheat, oats and barley for human consumption
within Canada and to establish voluntary marketing Commissions for pork and

Because of an anticipated 20 per cent drop in grain prices, most south

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There were discussions among the Parties that we would defer this vote until six o'clock on Monday. I have been advised by the Table Officers that according to Standing Order 13(2), it is not possible to delay this vote until Monday at six o'clock on the basis that the House knew when the motion would come to a vote.
However, I have been in the House for some eight years. There were a number of occasions when all the Parties agreed to a speech by one Member from each Party for up to one-half hour each, which provided for an hour and a half of debate. In my opinion, that was a fixed time and the bell should not have rung more than 15 minutes.
I believe the opposition Whip would confirm that in most cases the bell would ring for 30 minutes. Technically, if what 1 have been told today is correct, whenever there is agreement among all Parties for one speaker from each Party to speak, there should be a 15-minute bell and the vote may not be deferred until Monday at six o'clock.
When one reads the Standing Order carefully, one finds that it refers to a predetermined time. I maintain that providing for a speech by one Member from each Party results in a predetermined time. 1 believe this situation should be thoroughly reviewed.
In every case I have agreed to the request for a 30-minute bell. I believe there is an inaccuracy here which should be corrected.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The Chair intends to review the matter, thoroughly as the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) indicates. However, as far as this vote is concerned, if 1 have a request for a deferred vote, unless there is unanimous consent I will reject the request.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, can we establish in the future that whenever there is a predetermined time for one speech by one member from each Party, the vote will be taken in 15 minutes? speechtext: I would just like to say that the Government Whip and I had discussions earlier today and I told him that I saw no difficulty in giving my consent to postponing the vote until next Monday. I know, Mr. Speaker, that the Standing Orders do not allow the vote that you have to take after a 15-minute bell to be deferred. The rules are there. I do not want to change the rules tonight. I understand the predicament we are in, but I would give my consent to postponing the vote as an exception to the rules.

I want simply to make the case that we have been waiting, quite frankly, for months for this vote to take place. Earlier in the day we informed our caucus that as per the Standing Orders, the vote would be taking place today. We informed our Members of that. I was then informed earlier today that the Government had decided to defer the vote. It had decided to defer the vote. It was not a request. I said, quite frankly, that we had made a decision, so, Mr. Speaker, if in fact the request comes for unanimous consent to defer the vote, I am afraid, under the circumstances, I would be unable to give that consent.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
